subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Mullerian duct anomalies and genital homologs
vignette: A 32-year-old woman has a history of two second-trimester pregnancy losses. Hysterosalpingogram shows a single uterine cavity with a central filling defect dividing it, and patent fallopian tubes with intraperitoneal contrast spill. She is diagnosed with a congenital uterine anomaly.
question: Which uterine anomaly is most likely, and what is the appropriate surgical management?

options.text: Bicornuate uterus due to incomplete fusion; treated with uterine unification surgery
Uterus didelphys due to complete failure of fusion; no surgery indicated
Septate uterus due to incomplete resorption of the septum; treated with septoplasty
Septate uterus due to incomplete fusion of the Mullerian ducts; treated with septoplasty
Bicornuate uterus due to incomplete resorption of the septum; treated with septoplasty

explanation_correct: A septate uterus results from incomplete resorption of the central septum after Mullerian duct fusion, producing a single external uterine contour with a divided cavity (central filling defect on HSG). It is the most common Mullerian anomaly and is associated with recurrent pregnancy loss; treatment is hysteroscopic septoplasty. This is distinct from bicornuate uterus (incomplete fusion, two horns) and didelphys (complete failure of fusion, double uterus/cervix/vagina).

explanation_incorrect.A: Bicornuate uterus results from incomplete fusion, giving two separate horns with an external indentation; the single cavity with a central septum here indicates a septate uterus, managed by septoplasty rather than unification.
explanation_incorrect.B: Didelphys is complete failure of fusion with a double uterus, cervix, and vagina, not a single divided cavity with a central septum.
explanation_incorrect.D: A septate uterus arises from incomplete resorption of the septum, not incomplete fusion of the ducts (which is bicornuate).
explanation_incorrect.E: Incomplete resorption of the septum causes a septate, not bicornuate, uterus; bicornuate uteri result from incomplete fusion and are not treated with septoplasty.

educationalObjective: Septate uterus equals incomplete septum resorption, is the most common Mullerian anomaly, and is treated with septoplasty.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Mullerian duct anomalies and genital homologs
vignette: A 24-year-old woman has a double uterus, two cervices, and a vaginal septum on pelvic examination. She has had no pregnancy complications yet.
question: Which embryologic error produced this finding?

options.text: Complete failure of fusion of the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts
Incomplete fusion of the Mullerian ducts
Incomplete resorption of the uterine septum
Failure of the urogenital sinus to form the distal vagina

explanation_correct: Uterus didelphys results from complete failure of the two paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts to fuse, producing a double uterus, double cervix, and often a vaginal septum. Incomplete fusion produces a bicornuate uterus, and incomplete resorption of the septum produces a septate uterus. These Mullerian anomalies are associated with decreased fertility and an increased risk of spontaneous abortion, prematurity, FGR, and malpresentation.

explanation_incorrect.B: Incomplete fusion of the Mullerian ducts produces a bicornuate uterus with two horns, not the completely duplicated uterus, cervix, and vagina of didelphys.
explanation_incorrect.C: Incomplete resorption of the septum produces a septate uterus (single outer contour, divided cavity), not complete duplication.
explanation_incorrect.D: The distal vagina arises from the urogenital sinus; its failure would not produce a double uterus and two cervices.
explanation_incorrect.E: Persistence of Wolffian ducts gives Gartner duct cysts in females, not duplication of the uterus and cervix.

educationalObjective: Uterus didelphys reflects complete failure of Mullerian duct fusion, yielding double uterus, cervix, and vagina.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Mullerian duct anomalies and genital homologs
vignette: A 28-year-old woman undergoing infertility evaluation has a hysterosalpingogram. The report describes a normal-shaped uterine cavity and free spillage of contrast into the peritoneal cavity from both fallopian tubes.
question: What does intraperitoneal spill of contrast on hysterosalpingogram indicate?
explanation_correct: On hysterosalpingogram, a normal uterine cavity and intraperitoneal spill of contrast indicate that the fallopian tubes are patent, allowing contrast to pass through the tubes and spill into the peritoneal cavity. Absence of spill suggests tubal obstruction. This imaging is used to evaluate uterine structure and tubal patency in infertility.

explanation_incorrect.A: A septate uterus would appear as a filling defect dividing the uterine cavity, not as a normal cavity with free spill.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tubal obstruction would prevent contrast from spilling into the peritoneal cavity; the presence of spill indicates patency.
explanation_incorrect.C: HSG assesses anatomy (cavity shape and tubal patency), not whether ovulation is occurring.
explanation_incorrect.E: HSG is not used to detect pregnancy and does not indicate an intrauterine gestation.

educationalObjective: Free intraperitoneal contrast spill on HSG confirms patent fallopian tubes with a normal uterine cavity.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Mullerian duct anomalies and genital homologs
vignette: A medical student compares male and female external genitalia, noting that homologous structures arise from the same embryonic precursors but differentiate under different hormonal influences (DHT vs estrogen).
question: The glans penis and glans clitoris are homologous structures. From which embryonic precursor do both arise?
explanation_correct: The genital tubercle gives rise to the glans penis in males (under DHT) and the glans clitoris in females (under estrogen). The urogenital folds form the ventral penile urethra in males and the labia minora in females; the labioscrotal swellings form the scrotum and labia majora; and the urogenital sinus gives rise to the prostate/Cowper glands and the urethral/Skene and Bartholin glands.

explanation_incorrect.A: Urogenital folds form the ventral penile urethra and labia minora, not the glans.
explanation_incorrect.C: Labioscrotal swellings form the scrotum and labia majora, not the glans.
explanation_incorrect.D: The urogenital sinus forms the prostate, bulbourethral (Cowper) glands, and associated urethral glands, not the glans.
explanation_incorrect.E: The mesonephric duct forms the Wolffian-derived internal genitalia, not external genital structures.

educationalObjective: The genital tubercle is the common precursor of the glans penis and glans clitoris.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Mullerian duct anomalies and genital homologs
vignette: A researcher is mapping male-to-female genital homologs. She wants to identify the female structure homologous to the male bulbourethral (Cowper) gland, since both derive from the urogenital sinus.
question: Which female structure is homologous to the male bulbourethral (Cowper) gland?
explanation_correct: The urogenital sinus gives rise to the bulbourethral (Cowper) glands in males and the greater vestibular (Bartholin) glands in females, which are therefore homologous. The same sinus gives rise to the prostate in males and the urethral/paraurethral (Skene) glands in females. The urogenital folds form the ventral penile urethra and labia minora, the labioscrotal swellings form the scrotum and labia majora, and the genital tubercle forms the glans.

explanation_incorrect.A: The urethral and paraurethral (Skene) glands are the female homologs of the prostate, not of the Cowper glands.
explanation_incorrect.B: The labia minora derive from urogenital folds, homologous to the ventral penile urethra, not from urogenital-sinus gland precursors.
explanation_incorrect.C: The labia majora derive from labioscrotal swellings, homologous to the scrotum.
explanation_incorrect.D: The glans clitoris derives from the genital tubercle, homologous to the glans penis.

educationalObjective: The bulbourethral (Cowper) gland and greater vestibular (Bartholin) gland are urogenital-sinus-derived male/female homologs.
